---

### Survey of what the tree already holds

- **Patrick Flynn (I1):** birth ca. 1845 in Ireland (tree fact F1); death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, PA (F2, cited to S3, Pennsylvania death certificates). The objective says he was born in Pennsylvania, so the birthplace is in dispute.
- **Thomas Flynn (I2):** birth ca. 1818 in Ireland (F3), linked as Patrick's father (R1). That link rests on the 1850 census (S1), 1860 census (S2), and death certificate (S3).
- Only the 1850 census has extracted assertions. Its relationship fact (a_004) is inferred from household position, not stated. The 1860 census (S2) is cited but has no extracted assertion, and the timeline has a medium gap for 1851–1860.

---

### Plan pl_002 — eight items in execution order

| # | ID | Type | Place | Years | Repository | Purpose |
|---|-----|------|-------|-------|------------|---------|
| 1 | pli_004 | vital record | Schuylkill County | 1908 | State archives | Death certificate — check whether S3 is already in hand before searching |
| 2 | pli_005 | census | Schuylkill County | 1860 | FamilySearch | Fills the 1851–1860 gap; tests whether Patrick is still with Thomas |
| 3 | pli_006 | census | Schuylkill County | 1870 | FamilySearch | First census with relationship-to-head and birthplace; tests the Ireland vs. Pennsylvania conflict |
| 4 | pli_007 | census | Schuylkill County | 1870 | **Ancestry** | Your requested cross-check; fallback for pli_006, linked to the Ancestry 1870 collection |
| 5 | pli_008 | vital record | Pennsylvania | 1838–1846 | FamilySearch | Parents' marriage record — provides mother's maiden name |
| 6 | pli_009 | probate | Schuylkill County | 1850–1905 | County courthouse | Thomas's estate file at the Register of Wills; could name Patrick as an heir (browse-only image set) |
| 7 | pli_010 | church | Schuylkill County parish | 1844–1846 | Other | Catholic baptism naming both parents; access unknown |
| 8 | pli_011 | census | Schuylkill County | 1850 | FamilySearch | FAN item: households neighbouring Thomas's dwelling 84 |

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn died 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County (tree fact F2, cited to S3, Pennsylvania death certificates). A 1908 state death certificate postdates the 1906 start of statewide registration and usually names the decedent's father and mother. The tree cites S3 for the death but no assertion from it is in research.json, so first check whether that certificate is already in hand and extract its parent names if so; if not, locate it through the FamilySearch index 'Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999' (name-searchable) or the state record. Parent names on a certificate are direct but informant-dependent evidence, so test them against the other items.

Fills the 1851-1860 gap in timeline t_001 (medium severity; the 1860 census is not yet searched). Thomas Flynn (tree I2, born ca. 1818 Ireland) headed the 1850 Schuylkill household that held Patrick (age 5, dwelling 84). The tree cites the 1860 census as S2, but no 1860 assertion has been extracted. The 1860 household should show whether Patrick (about 15) is still with Thomas and whether the head's relationship to Patrick is stated. The FamilySearch 1860 United States census is name-searchable. Search by Patrick Flynn and by the Thomas Flynn household, since the given name may be spelled differently.

Patrick (about 25) is the first adult-age census appearance to test. The 1870 census is the first to record each person's relationship to the head of household and birthplace, which tests the Ireland (tree) versus Pennsylvania (objective) birthplace conflict for Patrick. The FamilySearch 1870 United States census is name-searchable. Search by Patrick Flynn and by Thomas Flynn's household, and check neighbouring dwellings if the family moved. Thomas's household may have changed, so a missing match is not proof of absence.

Requested cross-check of the 1870 census on Ancestry, the paid index for 1870 Pennsylvania (1870 United States Federal Census, name-searchable). It is a derivative index, so verify any hit against the original image. It serves as the fallback if the FamilySearch 1870 search in the prior item yields no match, since the same enumeration sits on both sites and the paid index may transcribe a name or place differently.

It does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Search 'Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991' (name-searchable) and the civil marriage collections. If Thomas's wife married before, each of her marriage records must be searched, because a surname on this marriage may be a prior married name.

Thomas Flynn (born ca. 1818) is the candidate father. His estate file at the Schuylkill County Register of Wills, if he died in the window, could name Patrick as a son or heir. The window runs from the 1850 census to about 1905, sized to Thomas's plausible lifespan, not to Patrick's research window. The Pennsylvania probate collection on FamilySearch is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Register of Wills dockets, not a name search. Records before 1811 sit under the parent counties.

Sacramental registers are held at the parish or the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county, and the county stayed under Philadelphia until 1961. entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn's death on 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County is already in the tree, sourced to a Pennsylvania death certificate, but the tree records no parent names from it. Patrick may have no baptism here if he was born in Ireland, so search for baptisms of Flynn children from about 1846 to 1865 naming Thomas Flynn and the mother as parents; the sponsors are FAN leads. Roman Catholic sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese, not the county, so a county hit is a lead to the parish register.

Dedicated parents' marriage item. Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900 and Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 are both name-searchable; search for Thomas Flynn as groom, about 1838-1846, since he was born about 1818 and Patrick about 1845. The marriage confirms the couple as a unit and, if this was the mother's first marriage, gives her maiden name. It dates the union but does not by itself prove Patrick is their child; a record placing Patrick with both parents is still needed. If no Pennsylvania entry exists, the marriage may have been in Ireland, which needs a locality survey first.

Companion to the parents' marriage item, testing whether that marriage was the mother's first. The mother's given name and maiden name are not in the tree, so search County Marriages, 1775-1991 (name-searchable) for a Flynn widow or remarriage after Thomas Flynn's death, and Marriages, 1709-1940 (name-searchable) for Thomas Flynn as a former husband. A remarriage under another surname means the earlier marriage record may not give her birth name.

Friends-and-neighbours item. The 1850 United States Census is name-searchable, and the Flynn household was at dwelling 84 (log_001, already searched for the 1850 question). Search the neighbouring dwellings and Irish-born households on the same page for kin of Thomas Flynn, who may name a sister, brother or aunt that would point to the mother's family. This is a new neighbour search, not a repeat of the subject search.

It states relationships, unlike 1850 where the son link is only inferred from household position, so it can show Patrick as Thomas Flynn's son and name the wife by given name. Patrick would be about 15.

The 1870 United States Census is name-searchable. Patrick would be about 25; a household that still holds the mother, or a widow with Thomas's surname, could name her and confirm the family unit after Thomas's probable death. Searched for the mother's name as a household member, which tests the widow remarriage item.

Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill Register of Wills dockets for Thomas Flynn, not a name search. The window is sized to Thomas's lifespan, not the subject's: born about 1818, so a death at any point up to about 1878 could leave an estate file. Patrick Flynn's own estate, if one was opened after his 1908 death. The same browse-only probate collection is an image browse. The file may name surviving heirs, including a mother or siblings, which tests the parent link from the other side. The window is sized to an administration following a 1908 death.

Fallback to the death certificate item. Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 are name-searchable. A burial entry for Thomas Flynn or the mother may state an age, a birthplace and a spouse name. This runs if the death certificate's parent fields are blank or illegible.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: A baptism of Patrick Flynn, born about 1845, would name his father and mother. The 1850 census (log_001) places Patrick in Thomas Flynn's household but gives his birthplace as Ireland, while the tree records Pennsylvania; the baptism tests which is right. The Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection is name-searchable. Per the locality entry, Catholic registers are held at the parish or the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, so if the index is silent, check the parish register.

Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother, dated before Patrick's birth, would confirm the couple as a unit and may give the mother's maiden name. The marriage shows the couple married, not that Patrick is their child; a baptism or household record must place him with them. The Pennsylvania County Marriages and Civil Marriages collections are name-searchable. The marriage may have occurred in Ireland, which this Pennsylvania plan does not cover.

A Catholic marriage register entry for Thomas Flynn is a second route to the parents' marriage and the mother's maiden name. The Pennsylvania Church Marriages collection is name-searchable, though the parish register itself may be held only at the parish or the Archdiocese of Philadelphia.

Thomas Flynn's wife may have married before or after Thomas. A remarriage or earlier marriage would show a different surname and could change which candidate is the mother. The Pennsylvania County Marriages collection is name-searchable. Search for the wife by her given name with Flynn and with any other surname the 1860 and 1870 households show her under.

Neighbours and households near dwelling 84 in the 1850 census may include Thomas Flynn's siblings or other Irish-born kin, who would be the FAN evidence this parentage question requires. The United States Census 1850 collection is name-searchable. Read the neighbouring dwellings for Flynn and other Irish-born families with Thomas's age and wife's given name.

The 1860 census records relationships, so it can confirm whether Patrick is Thomas's son and name Thomas's wife, Patrick's mother. The United States Census 1860 collection is name-searchable. The tree cites the 1860 census, but no extracted assertion from it is in the project yet.

The 1870 and 1880 censuses show whether the mother is a widow, the household's relationships, and, in 1880, the birthplaces of Patrick's parents. The United States Census 1870 and 1880 collections are name-searchable. A widowed mother living with Patrick would give a second route to her name.

A will or administration for Thomas Flynn, or for his widow, would name the heirs, and Patrick would be among them if he is their son. The date window is sized to Thomas's lifespan (born about 1818), since the estate could be filed any time from Patrick's birth to about 1905. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill County Register of Wills dockets, and the access route is unknown.

Patrick's 1908 death in Schuylkill County has a state certificate, since statewide registration began in 1906. The certificate may name his parents and birthplace. The Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials collection is name-searchable. Check the parents and birthplace fields on the certificate itself, which the tree's death source (S3) may already hold without those details.

Burial records may place Patrick in a family plot with Thomas Flynn or with the mother, which would link them. The Pennsylvania Cemetery Records collection is name-searchable. A burial entry may also give an age or a birthplace that tests the Ireland-or-Pennsylvania conflict.

entry.rationale: The 1850 census household of Thomas and Sarah Hale should list every child at home with age and birthplace, so it is the fastest way to test for children beyond the five in the tree. Collection is name-searchable. Children born 1836-1847 are expected; a child born before 1836 or after 1847 would also appear here if living at home.

The 1860 household shows children still at home after 1850 and any child born between the 1850 and 1860 censuses. Collection is name-searchable. Ages should be checked against the 1850 entry to catch children who left or died in between.

The 1870 census, taken after Thomas Hale's 1868 death, shows Sarah's household and any children still living with her. Collection is name-searchable. Children may have married or moved out by then, so this item tests survivors rather than completeness.

The 1830 and 1840 federal censuses name only the head of household and count the rest by age bracket. They can show whether Thomas and Sarah already had children before Mary, who is the earliest known child (born about 1836). Both collections are name-searchable.

If Sarah was living in 1880 (she is a widow after Thomas's 1868 death), her household may include unmarried or dependent children or grandchildren. Collection is name-searchable. This is a lower-yield check than the decennial censuses above.

The marriage of Thomas Hale and Sarah, likely before Mary's birth of about 1836, fixes the start of the couple's childbearing and may give Sarah's maiden name. Ohio County Marriages is name-searchable for Greene County from 1803. If this is not Sarah's first marriage, a later record may be needed, and this item does not settle it alone.

Ohio Births and Christenings (1821-1962) is name-searchable. Searching for children with Thomas and Sarah Hale as parents may find baptisms or births of children not in the tree, including any born outside the 1836-1847 span. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

The 1880 census is the first federal schedule that states each person's relationship to the head of household, so it can directly test whether Patrick is recorded as a son of Thomas Flynn (b. about 1818, Ireland), who headed the Schuylkill County household in 1850 and 1860. The United States census collection for 1880 is name-searchable. Search Patrick Flynn with birth about 1845 and birthplace Ireland or Pennsylvania, since the 1850 census and the 1908 death certificate disagree on birthplace. Also search Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County to see whether he heads a household or is a relative in another household.

The 1870 schedule does not state relationships, so any match is inferred from household position, age and surname, as in the 1850 and 1860 records. Search Flynn and variant spellings (Flinn, Flynne), and check whether Thomas Flynn (about 52) heads a household containing Patrick or a separate household next to it.

Patrick is alive here (about 55; he died in 1908), so this is the last census in which he could appear as an adult. The United States census collection for 1900 is name-searchable. Thomas Flynn (about 82) may be dead by 1900, so a household headed by Patrick or a relative may show Thomas as a resident parent, or may show Patrick alone. Test both possibilities.

Associates (FAN) item, required on a parentage question. If Thomas Flynn does not head a household with Patrick in 1880, the records of the Flynn households on the same enumeration pages, and of the households Patrick is shown next to, may show Thomas living as a boarder, lodger or relative, or show a shared household of Irish-born neighbours with the same origin. Use the 1880 schedule's neighbour order for Patrick's dwelling, and record the Flynn households found alongside it.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

The 1850 and 1860 placements (a_004, a_010 in ps_001) are inferred from position and surname only. An 1880 entry listing Patrick as son of Thomas Flynn would turn indirect evidence into direct evidence. Collection is name-searchable.

The 1870 census is an unsearched gap listed in ps_001. It names every household member, so it can give Thomas Flynn's wife by first name and test whether Patrick is still in the household at about age 25. Compare the dwelling with the 1850 (dwelling 84, log_001) and 1860 (dwelling 112, log_004) households. Collection is name-searchable.

The 1900 census is an unsearched gap listed in ps_001. Patrick would be about 55 and Thomas Flynn (born about 1818) may still be living. The 1900 schedule gives each member's relationship to head and a mother's child count, which can test the parentage and the mother's family. Collection is name-searchable.

The Pennsylvania mortality schedules (1850-1880) can show whether Thomas Flynn died before 1880, which bounds the probate and later census search. A death entry naming a son Patrick or a wife would also be direct evidence. Collection is name-searchable.

Thomas Flynn's marriage before Patrick's birth (about 1845) is needed to identify the mother's maiden name. Schuylkill County has existed since 1811, so the marriage would be filed there. The county marriage collection is name-searchable. Read the bondsmen and witnesses as FAN names, since they are often the bride's relatives.

Patrick's baptism would name both parents. The census gives Ireland as his birthplace, but the 1908 death certificate says Pennsylvania, so the baptism may be in either place. Nothing in the plan has a fallback relationship. Items 1 to 4 and 8 to 11 are unsearched, so the question is still open.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.guide_markdown:
## Lincolnshire, England - 1750-1800

FamilySearch's 'England, Births and Christenings' collection (1473014) is a partial Legacy index: it does not index all records for this place or period, and no records or corrections are being added — a nil there is a statement about the index, not proof that no christening exists; search the parish register itself before concluding absence. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England,_Births_and_Christenings_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records)

entry.rationale: Mary Dawson's own christening is the record most likely to name her parents. The tree holds only an unsourced birth fact of about 1772 in Lincolnshire. Search the England, Births and Christenings collection (1473014), which is name-searchable. Per loc_001 it is a partial Legacy index, so a miss does not prove no christening exists; the parish register itself must be checked before absence is concluded.

Fallback for item 1: if the indexed christening does not turn up, browse the Lincolnshire parish baptism registers for the window page by page. volume_search returned no Lincolnshire volumes this session, so the county record office holding the registers must be identified from the locality guide before this browse runs.

Parentage test: the marriage of Mary's candidate parents, dated before her birth of about 1772. It gives the mother's maiden name and corroborates a father, but it does not alone show that Mary is their child; a christening or household record placing her with them is still needed. Search the England, Births and Christenings collection (1473014) and then the parish marriage register image. Keep the search on the surname only until a record names the parents.

FAN item: baptisms of Mary's siblings, who would be christened in the same parish with the same parents named. A sibling's entry names the parents directly, and godparents or witnesses point to kin. Window sized to the children of a couple married about 1755-1772. Search the christening collection (1473014) and the parish register image, not the subject's name alone.

Mary's own burial or death entry, and her marriage entry, which state an age, a home parish or a birthplace. This matters because the christening may not survive or may not be indexed. Use the register-start date of the parish, taken from the locality guide, to decide whether a christening is even expected. Search the Lincolnshire parish registers held by the county record office, after identifying it from the locality guide.

Candidate father's will or administration, if he died while his children were young. The window is sized to a father of a child born about 1772, who could die anywhere from about 1772 to about 1830, not to Mary's own research window. A will naming Mary or her siblings is direct parentage evidence. Lincolnshire probate records sit with the ecclesiastical courts; the repository must be confirmed from the locality guide.

items.guide_markdown:
## Württemberg, Germany - 1780-1830

German children baptised with two or more given names were often called by the second in daily life (the wiki's example: Johann Christoph and Johann Friedrich were usually called Christoph and Friedrich) — search later records under the second given name alone as well as the full baptismal name. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Naming_Customs)

entry.rationale: Baptism of Anna Margaretha Bauer, born 1792. The tree holds only a birth fact (1792, Württemberg), with no source and no relatives. A baptism entry names the father and mother, the most direct route to the parentage question. Search Germany, Births and Baptisms, 1558-1898 (name-searchable, per loc_001). Per loc_001's quirk, also search under the second given name Margaretha alone. Later items depend on the parents' names this record gives.

Fallback for item 1 if the name-searchable baptism index returns nothing. Browse the image group of the Württemberg parish baptism register for 1791-1793 (browse-only), page by page, for the parish identified from the birth place, and read the entries for early 1792 by hand. Catalog tools returned no Württemberg volume this session, so the exact register must be located first. Also checks any index hit from item 1 against the original image.

Parents' marriage. Once item 1 or 2 names the father and mother, search Germany Marriages, 1558-1929 (name-searchable, per loc_001) for that couple. The marriage gives the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage, and it corroborates the father by date, but it does not by itself establish that Anna Margaretha is their child; a baptism or household record placing her with them is still needed.

Companion to item 3: the mother's other marriages. A surname given by one marriage record may be a prior married name, so search Germany Marriages, 1558-1929 (name-searchable) under the mother's given name for any other marriage, including a remarriage after the father's death. Each marriage record found is checked for the mother's birth surname.

FAN item. Baptisms of Anna Margaretha's siblings, and the godparents named in item 1's record, search Germany, Births and Baptisms, 1558-1898 (name-searchable). A sibling's baptism names the same parents and so tests the parentage independently of item 1. Godparents often are relatives, and a sibling's entry can confirm the family unit.

The subject's own marriage. Search Germany Marriages, 1558-1929 (name-searchable) for Anna Margaretha Bauer. A marriage entry often states her age, home parish or birthplace, and sometimes her parents' names. This is independent of item 1 and can run in parallel with it.

The subject's own death or burial entry, in the parish where she last lived. Death entries often state an age, a home parish or a birthplace, which can give an origin the birth register cannot. The locality entry lists no death or burial collection, and the catalog tools returned no Württemberg collection this session, so confirm access before relying on it.

Estate, guardianship or division records for the father, if item 3 identifies him. A guardianship or estate file names minor children and their mother, independent of the church registers. The window runs to about 60 years after the 1792 birth, because a father's estate may be settled decades after death. Access is not verified this session; the Landesarchiv Baden-Württemberg is the likely holder, to be confirmed.

## Locality Guide: Trysil, Hedmark, Norway (1780–1880)

### Jurisdictional Context

Trysil became its own *prestegjeld* in 1780, separated from Elverum. The 1860 death falls squarely within Trysil's own records. Administratively: Amt of Hedmark from 1781; Sorenskriveri of Søndre Østerdalen; Diocese of Oslo/Christiania 1537–1864, then Hamar.

### Church Records — Primary Source

- **Digitized images** (browse-only, 0% name-indexed): Kirkebøker 1588–1928 (Trysil prestegjeld) at FamilySearch Catalog (cat. 737) and Digitalarkivet. The 1860 burial will be in volume 008679203_003 (1814–1877, 325 images).
- **Indexed national extracts** (name-searchable): Norway Burials 1666–1927 (FS col 1468081; also Ancestry, MyHeritage); Norway Baptisms 1634–1927 (FS col 1467014); Norway Marriages 1660–1926 (FS col 1468080).
- **Dissenter church**: Trysil Frimenighet 1858–1920 at Digitalarkivet (images).

### Census

| Year | FS Collection | Access | Notes |
|------|--------------|--------|-------|
| 1801 | 3733603 | indexed & images | Subject ~21; also Ancestry, MyHeritage |
| 1865 | 3756102 | indexed & images | Postdates death; shows widow/children |
| 1870 | 4135961 | indexed & images | Postdates death |
| 1875 | 1529106 | indexed & images | Postdates death; also Ancestry, MyHeritage |

### Probate

- Norway Probate Index Cards 1640–1903 (FS col 1661306): indexed — locate the 1860 estate filing here.
- Skifteprotokoller image volumes at FS Catalog cover through 1853; post-1853 volumes held at Riksarkivet/Digitalarkivet.

### Land Records

- Pantebøker (mortgage/property) 1712–1860 (FS Catalog 489152) — images.

### Military / Levy Rolls

Norway's conscription/levy rolls (*lægdsruller*) began 1789. Each enrolled boy is listed under his father's name — direct parentage evidence. A male born ~1780 would appear from approximately 1789. Access via Riksarkivet and Digitalarkivet.

### Farm Books (*Bygdebøker*)

Trysilboka (Lillevold, Larsen, Bryn; FS Library 948.23/T2 D2l) — multiple volumes covering farm histories and resident genealogies for Trysil with personal name indexes in volumes 1–3, 7–8. High-value source for locating a household at the farm level.

### Key Access Points

- **FamilySearch** (free): indexed burials/baptisms/marriages/census, browse church record images
- **Digitalarkivet** (free): church books at media.digitalarkivet.no/en/kb/browse
- **Ancestry** (subscription): Norway Burials/Baptisms/Marriages extracts, 1865 census
- **MyHeritage** (subscription): Norway Burials/Marriages, 1865/1875 census
- **FamilySearch Library** (on-site or center): Trysilboka farm book, catalog microfilm

items.guide_markdown:
## Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico - 1880-1920

Although Mexicans use two surnames, most indexed records carry only the first (paternal) surname — search with the paternal surname alone; when the person is not found, search through the parents (a parent search with each parent's first surname, leaving out the child's name). (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Improve_your_Search_Results_for_Hispanic_Ancestors_in_FamilySearch.org)

entry.rationale: A civil birth registration of the subject, about 1895, would name both parents. The Jalisco civil registration collection (1857-2000) is name-searchable per loc_001. Search the given name Guadalupe with the paternal surname Hernández alone, since most indexed records carry only the first surname (loc_001 quirk). The subject's second surname, Ramírez, is the mother's surname under the Mexico Naming Customs wiki page; this is a lead to test, not a settled fact.

A baptism entry in the Guadalajara parish registers would name the parents and godparents. The Jalisco Catholic Church Records collection (1590-2022) is name-searchable per loc_001. Search Guadalupe with Hernández alone. This is co-equal with the civil birth record, since civil registration in 1895 may be incomplete.

Fallback for the Guadalajara baptism search: the national Mexico, Baptisms, 1560-1950 collection is name-searchable per loc_001 and may index a parish entry the Jalisco Catholic collection does not surface. It names the same parents as the Jalisco baptism entry.

The parents' marriage record would confirm the couple as a unit, and if it is the mother's first marriage it gives her maiden name. Her maiden name is only a lead from the subject's second surname Ramírez, so a search keyed on that surname asserts nothing. The window is sized to the mother's likely childbearing years, not the subject's. A marriage alone does not prove the subject is their child; a birth or baptism entry must place her with them. Search the Jalisco civil registration collection (name-searchable per loc_001) with Hernández as groom surname and Ramírez as bride surname.

Fallback for the parents' civil marriage search: the church marriage register in the Jalisco Catholic Church Records collection (name-searchable per loc_001) records a Catholic marriage that may have no civil entry indexed. It is the church counterpart to the civil marriage and supplies the bride's maiden surname if this was her first marriage.

The subject's own marriage record, dated to the years she would have married, usually names her parents. The subject is a woman who kept her maiden surname (Mexico Naming Customs), so search her under Hernández. The Jalisco civil registration collection is name-searchable per loc_001. It is a separate source for the parents' names, independent of birth and baptism.

The subject's death record, dated after her birth window, usually names her parents and her age. The window reaches the later years a death could fall in, not only the birth estimate. Search Jalisco civil registration (1918187), and the national Mexico, Deaths, 1680-1940 collection (name-searchable per loc_001) as a second check for deaths through 1940.

Full-text co-occurrence search of Hernández and Ramírez as separate terms across Guadalajara-area baptism and burial texts, routed to search-full-text. This is the route when the parents are not named in an indexed field: the parents' own acts, and the baptisms of the subject's siblings, would name both surnames together. It is also the FAN route, since godparents and witnesses named alongside the couple may point back to the family. Run it unscoped to a collection.

items.guide_markdown:
## Hamre prestegjeld, Hordaland, Norway - 1765-1800

Norwegian name spellings were set by the recorder and vary between records (the wiki's example: the given name Sivert written as Syver, Sjur, Siver, Sifuer or Siffuer) — search given-name spelling variants, not just the tree's spelling, before concluding a nil. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Church_Records)

entry.rationale: Direct search for Unna Halsteinsdatter as bride in the Hamre parish marriage records. Meland, and its farm Hestdal, was an annex parish (sokn) of Hamre, so its marriages are in the Hamre kirkebøker. Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926 (collection 1468080) is name-searchable. Search her name in variant forms (Unna, Unne, Una, Onne) with the surname Halsteinsdatter, including abbreviated forms (d., dr., dtr.) and the patronymic alone, because spelling was not standardized before 1917. Per the naming-customs page, her surname is patronymic from her father Halstein, and the husband may be recorded by a farm name rather than a surname. The window 1763-1805 covers a first marriage from about age 18 to 60.

Fallback for pli_001. If the indexed marriage search returns nothing, browse the Hamre kirkebøker marriage and banns (lysing) image volumes page by page for the window. This is browse-only, not a name search. No image group for this place was returned by the volume search this session, so the volume must be identified in the FamilySearch catalog for Hamre prestegjeld before browsing. Banns name the bride and groom before the wedding and can show a marriage the index omits.

FAN and parentage context. Norway Baptisms, 1634-1927 (collection 1467014) is name-searchable. Find Unna's own baptism and her siblings' baptisms in Meland to name her parents, Halstein and his wife, and the siblings. Siblings' marriage and burial entries, and sponsors, can name her in later records, so this widens the search for the marriage without assuming it. Pursue after pli_001 so the family names are known for the marriage search.

Covers a later or second marriage. The locality entry's period ends in 1800, and by 1800 she was about 55. A marriage after the period, or a remarriage after the husband's death, would fall outside the 1765-1800 window. Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926 (collection 1468080) is name-searchable, so search the same name variants as pli_001.

**What the project already has:**

6. **Marriage records, Schuylkill, 1840–1880** — covers any Pennsylvania marriage of Thomas, identifies a second wife
7. **Cemetery burials, Schuylkill, 1845–1908** — FAN cluster item
8. **Mortality schedules, 1850–1880** — checks for a household death of a possible mother or sibling
9. **Naturalization, Thomas Flynn, 1845–1880** — confirms Thomas's origins; note to verify the district first

**Gap flagged:** The parents' marriage likely occurred in Ireland before emigration. A locality survey for Ireland is needed before Irish baptism/marriage records can be planned. That can be addressed by running a **locality-guide** for Ireland.

**Next step:** Execute the plan, beginning with item 1 (the 1908 death record), using **search-records** for FamilySearch items.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Greene County probate has been held by the Greene County Probate Court since 1852 (loc_001), so an 1868 estate file for Thomas Hale would be filed there. The Ohio Probate Records collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county dockets, not a name search. An estate file may name his heirs and their residence, including a Pennsylvania origin. Run it after item 1, which may supply names to look for.

The 1850 United States Census is name-searchable nationally. It records birthplace only as a state, so it cannot give a county. It places Thomas in Greene County with a Pennsylvania-born household, fixes his age against the c.1810 birth estimate, and lists neighbours. Neighbours who share a Pennsylvania origin can be traced to a county of birth (FAN).

The Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection (1709-1950) is name-searchable statewide. A baptism would name the parish, and the parish location gives the county of birth.
